# Inference in Production {#sec-eng-inference}

Inference is where a trained model meets real traffic. This chapter treats
serving as an engineering discipline: turning a model artifact into a
service that answers within a latency budget, under concurrency, at a cost
you can defend.

By the end you will be able to size a serving deployment, reason about the
throughput and latency trade-off, and instrument a model endpoint so you
can see what it is doing.

## The serving problem

What a request actually costs, where the time goes, and why naive
request-per-process serving leaves most of the hardware idle.

## Batching and scheduling

Static versus continuous batching, the queueing that sits in front of the
accelerator, and the point where batching stops paying for itself.

## Memory and the KV cache

Why the key-value cache dominates memory for autoregressive models, paged
attention, and eviction under pressure.

## Quantization and compilation

Trading precision for speed and footprint, graph compilation, and how to
tell whether an optimization preserved the outputs you care about.

## Scaling out

Replication, autoscaling on the right signal, multi-accelerator sharding,
and routing across heterogeneous hardware.

## Observability and reliability

The metrics that matter (latency percentiles, tokens per second, cost per
request), load shedding, timeouts, and graceful degradation.
